subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: What is the number of molecules in 0.250 mol of CO₂? (Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³)
items.note: N = n × Nᴀ = 0.250 × 6.02×10²³ = 1.505×10²³ ≈ 1.51×10²´ (3 s.f.). Watch the exponent — 1.50×10²³ forgets the 0.250 multiplier's effect on magnitude.

items.stem: How many oxygen atoms are present in 0.100 mol of Al₂(SO₄)₃? (Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³)
items.note: Each formula unit has 12 O atoms (4 × 3): 0.100 × 12 = 1.20 mol O atoms → 1.20 × 6.02×10²³ = 7.22×10²³. The trap is counting O once instead of four times per sulfate ion.

items.stem: The empirical formula of a compound containing 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass is:
What mass of NaCl (M = 58.44 g/mol) is needed to prepare 250.0 cm³ of a 0.100 mol/dm³ solution?
items.note: n = c×V = 0.100 × 0.2500 = 0.0250 mol → m = 0.0250 × 58.44 = 1.46 g. The cm³ → dm³ division by 1000 is the classic slip.

items.stem: In the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, what is the maximum mass of NH₃ (M = 17.0 g/mol) from 14.0 g N₂ and excess H₂?
items.note: n(N₂) = 14.0/28.0 = 0.500 mol → 1.00 mol NH₃ → 17.0 g. Ratio 1:2 from the equation.

items.stem: 5.60 g of iron (M = 55.8 g/mol) reacts completely with chlorine: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. What mass of FeCl₃ (M = 162.2 g/mol) forms?
25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH exactly neutralises 20.0 cm³ of HCl. The concentration of the HCl is:
Which sample contains the greatest number of atoms?
items.note: H₂O = 3 atoms/unit → 3.0 mol atoms; CO₂ = 3 → 3.0; C₂H₆ = 8 × 0.5 = 4.0; O₂ = 2. Recheck: C₂H₆ gives 4.0 mol atoms — the greatest here is C₂H₆. (If you answered H₂O, recount atoms per molecule.)

items.stem: The Avogadro constant is best described as the number of:
choices: particles in 22.4 dm³ of any gas
particles in one mole of substance
items.note: Definition question — one mole contains 6.02×10²³ particles. 22.4 dm³ only applies to gases at STP with the old convention.

items.stem: 0.500 mol of an ideal gas occupies 12.3 dm³ at 300 K. The pressure is approximately:
items.note: PV = nRT → P = nRT/V = 0.500 × 8.31 × 300 / 0.0123 ≈ 1.01×10⁵ Pa = 101 kPa. Convert dm³ → m³ before using R = 8.31 J/(mol·K).

items.stem: What is the percentage yield if 8.0 g of product is obtained when the theoretical yield is 10.0 g?
items.note: %yield = actual/theoretical × 100 = 8.0/10.0 × 100 = 80%. Yields above 100% indicate impure product.

items.stem: A 2.00 g sample of an oxide of copper contains 1.60 g Cu. The empirical formula is (M: Cu 63.5, O 16.0):
items.note: Cu: 1.60/63.5 = 0.0252 mol; O: 0.40/16.0 = 0.0250 mol → 1:1 → CuO. The oxygen mass is what's left after Cu.

items.stem: Which change doubles the volume occupied by a fixed amount of ideal gas at constant pressure?
choices: Halving the pressure at constant T
Doubling the pressure at constant T
items.note: V ∝ T(K) at constant P — Kelvin, never Celsius. Option 3 also doubles V: halving P at constant T doubles V — but the stem fixes pressure, so only T doubling qualifies.

items.stem: The molar mass of a hydrated salt CuSO₄·5H₂O (Cu 63.5, S 32.1, O 16.0, H 1.0) is:
items.note: CuSO₄ = 63.5+32.1+64 = 159.6; 5H₂O = 90 → 249.6 g/mol. Forgetting waters of crystallisation is a classic Paper 1A trap.

items.stem: How many moles of ions are present in 1.0 mol of Ca(NO₃)₂ dissolved in water?
items.note: Ca(NO₃)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2NO₃⁻ = 3 mol ions per mol salt.

items.stem: 10.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄ is diluted to 100.0 cm³. The new concentration is:
items.note: Dilution factor 10 → c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ → 0.500×10.0/100.0 = 0.0500 mol/dm³. Keep the trailing zeros — they show the 3 s.f. precision.

items.stem: Which contains 0.0500 mol of particles?
items.note: 0.0500 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²². Exponent slips here are the most common Paper 1A error in stoichiometry.

items.stem: 2.00 g of a Group 2 metal reacts with excess water to give 0.0500 mol of H₂. The metal is (M: Mg 24.3, Ca 40.1, Sr 87.6, Ba 137.3):
items.note: M + 2H₂O → M(OH)₂ + H₂ gives 1 mol H₂ per mol metal: n(M) = 0.0500 mol → M = 2.00/0.0500 = 40.1 g/mol → calcium.

items.stem: The concentration of 5.85 g NaCl (M = 58.5) made up to 500 cm³ solution is:
items.note: n = 0.100 mol in 0.500 dm³ → c = 0.200 mol/dm³.

items.stem: Equal masses of CO and CO₂ contain which ratio of molecules CO : CO₂?
items.note: Same mass m: n ∝ 1/M → ratio CO:CO₂ = M(CO₂):M(CO) = 44:28 = 11:7. Inverting the ratio is the trap.

items.stem: 1.20 g of calcium carbonate is completely dissolved in 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. Determine which reactant is in excess. (M: CaCO₃ = 100.1)
markscheme: CaCO₃ + 2HCl: acid needed = 2 × 0.0120 = 0.0240 < 0.0250 mol available → acid in excess (1)
items.tactic: Limiting-reagent logic: convert both to moles, scale by the equation ratio, compare.

items.stem: A 0.250 g sample of an unknown acid H₂X requires 20.00 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ NaOH for complete neutralisation: H₂X + 2NaOH → Na₂X + 2H₂O. Determine the molar mass of H₂X.
items.tactic: Titration back-calculation: always start from the known solution, apply the equation ratio, then M = m/n with the sample mass.

items.stem: Element X has two isotopes: ⁷⁵X (50%) and ⁷⁷X (50%). Its relative atomic mass is:
items.note: Weighted mean: (75×50 + 77×50)/100 = 76. Abundances weight the average — never just average the mass numbers.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: Equal volumes of hydrogen and oxygen gases at the same temperature and pressure contain:
items.note: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of MOLECULES — not atoms or mass.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂O and a molar mass of 180 g/mol. Its molecular formula is:
items.note: M(CH₂O) = 30; n = 180/30 = 6 → molecular formula = (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose).
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: 12 g of carbon reacts with 48 g of oxygen: C + O₂ → CO₂ (M: C 12, O 16). Which reactant is limiting?
choices: Carbon — 1 mol vs 1.5 mol O₂ and the ratio needs 1:1
items.note: n(C) = 1 mol, n(O₂) = 3 mol. Ratio 1:1 → carbon limits (oxygen in excess). Calculate moles of BOTH before deciding.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: The percentage by mass of calcium in CaCO₃ (Ca 40.1, C 12.0, O 16.0) is approximately:
items.note: M(CaCO₃) = 100.1; %Ca = 40.1/100.1 × 100 ≈ 40%. Composition questions start from the molar mass.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: The molar volume of ANY ideal gas at STP (first assessment 2025 data booklet) is approximately:
items.note: The 2025+ data booklet value: 22.7 dm³/mol at STP (100 kPa, 273 K). Older books said 22.4 — use the booklet.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: The concentration of a solution in g/dm³ can be converted to mol/dm³ by dividing by:
items.note: c(g/dm³) ÷ M(g/mol) = c(mol/dm³). Watch the direction: g → mol divides by M.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: A 4.0 g sample of helium (M = 4.0 g/mol) contains how many atoms? (Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³)
items.note: n = 4.0/4.0 = 1 mol → 6.02×10²³ atoms. Helium is monatomic — atoms = moles directly.
items.topicLabel: Structure 1 — Stoichiometry & the particulate nature of matter

items.stem: Chlorine has two isotopes: ³⁵Cl (75%) and ³⁷Cl (25%). Its relative atomic mass is:
items.note: Weighted mean: (35×75 + 37×25)/100 = 35.5. Isotopic abundances weight the average — never take the simple mean of mass numbers.

items.stem: The number of molecules in 9.0 g of water (M = 18.0 g/mol) is: (Nᴀ = 6.02 × 10²³)
The total number of atoms in 0.50 mol of H₂O is:
items.note: 3 atoms per molecule × 0.50 mol = 1.5 mol atoms = 9.03×10²³. Count atoms per unit before multiplying.

items.stem: The volume occupied by 0.25 mol of any ideal gas at STP is approximately: (molar volume = 22.7 dm³/mol)
items.note: 0.25 × 22.7 = 5.7 dm³. Use the current data booklet value — older books said 22.4.

items.stem: 50 cm³ of H₂ react with 50 cm³ of Cl₂ at the same temperature and pressure: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. The volume of HCl formed is:
items.note: Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes: gas volume ratios = mole ratios. 1:1:2 → equal volumes of H₂ and Cl₂ give double the HCl volume.

items.stem: The percentage by mass of oxygen in CaCO₃ (Ca 40.1, C 12.0, O 16.0) is approximately:
items.note: 3 × 16.0 = 48.0 out of 100.1 → 48%. Three oxygens per formula unit — multiply before dividing.

items.stem: A compound contains 27.3% carbon and 72.7% oxygen by mass. Its empirical formula is: (C 12, O 16)
items.note: C: 27.3/12 = 2.275; O: 72.7/16 = 4.54 → ratio 1:2 → CO₂. Divide each percentage by the atomic mass, then simplify.

items.stem: 100 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is diluted to 500 cm³. The new concentration is:
items.note: c₁V₁ = c₂V₂: 2.0 × 100/500 = 0.40 mol/dm³. Dilution ×5 → concentration ÷5.

items.stem: 12.5 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO₄·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass. The remaining anhydrous CuSO₄ has a mass of 8.00 g. Determine the value of x. (M: CuSO₄ = 159.6, H₂O = 18.0)
items.tactic: Hydrated-salt problems: mass lost = water; convert both to moles and take the ratio. This is the classic experimental determination of x.

items.stem: A student needs 250 cm³ of 0.500 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate solution for a titration series. Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, that must be dissolved to prepare this solution. (Na 23.0, C 12.0, O 16.0)
items.tactic: Standard-solution preparation: moles from c×V, then mass from n×M. This exact calculation is what she'll do in the January titration practicals.
